detail.abstract: Recent theoretical studies have highlighted that both the level of public debt and the unit cost of servicing the debt (r-g) play a role in the sustainability of public finances. This paper builds on this literature and introduces a new approach to analysing the relationship between economic downturns and sovereign debt risks by considering the total public debt burden, that is, the interaction between the level of debt and r-g. We conduct this analysis for 18 advanced economies over a span of 150 years, uncovering three novel findings. First, we document that the level of public debt and the interest-growth differential convey distinct information about public finances conditions, reinforcing the argument for incorporating both measures in the assessment of sovereign debt sustainability risks. Second, we offer a long-term historical perspective on the role of the total public debt burden in shaping the severity of recessions and the pace of subsequent recoveries. Our findings demonstrate that a high public debt burden is associated with deeper economic contractions, sharper declines in investment, deflationary pressures and pronounced credit contractions during recessions. Further analysis of plausible transmission mechanisms suggests that an elevated total debt burden at the onset of recessions is linked to more limited accommodative policies during financial crises. Third, we document the feedback effects of financial crises on the components of the total public debt burden, demonstrating that both the level and cost of public debt systematically deteriorate, thereby heightening the risk of sovereign debt crises in the aftermath of financial turmoil.

title: Fiscal Stimulus and Housing Booms: Evidence from the 2003 Tax Cuts
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh - Katz Graduate School of Business,  and School of Business, University of Kansas

detail.title: Fiscal Stimulus and Housing Booms: Evidence from the 2003 Tax Cuts

keywords: Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the Bush-era tax cuts contributed to the U.S. housing boom that preceded the Great Recession. We focus on the 2003 reductions in dividend and capital gains tax rates and use a difference-in-differences design that exploits cross county variation in stock market exposure to identify the effects. Counties more exposed to the tax cuts experienced significantly faster house price growth after 2003 and greater housing activity, including home purchases and improvements-particularly for investment properties. We uncover a novel portfolio rebalancing channel linking equity payouts to housing demand, suggesting that the surge in corporate distributions following the tax cuts amplified their impact on house prices. Complementary evidence indicates that the concurrent reduction in regular income taxes also stimulated housing demand. Taken together, the findings imply that the Bush-era tax cuts played a meaningful role in fueling the early-2000s housing boom and highlight housing as an important transmission channel of fiscal stimulus.

title: Impact of UPI-Based Digital Transactions on Consumer Behaviour in India
affiliations: The International School Of Bangalore

detail.title: Impact of UPI-Based Digital Transactions on Consumer Behaviour in India
detail.abstract: The widespread use of digital payment technologies like Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has transformed Indian consumers' financial behaviours. This study looks at the effects of UPI adoption on consumer spending, savings, and habits like overspending. The study examines the psychological and economic mechanisms behind this shift using survey data from 169 participants. Behavioural finance concepts like the 'pain of paying' and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) are also used to understand the behavioural tendencies of UPI users. The results show that, especially among middle-class and digitally literate users, UPI adoption is linked to higher spending frequency, lower savings, and more impulsive spending behaviour. The paper concluded with policy recommendations to strike a balance between consumer protection and financial inclusion in India's rapidly digitizing economy.

detail.abstract: The eruption of war in Sudan in April 2023, marked by battles between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the ethnically rooted Rapid Support Forces (RSF), signifies a pivotal shift in regional security. Notably, the RSF's recruitment of Arab fighters from the Baggara Belt, spanning Chad, Niger, and Libya, represents a new phenomenon-transnational ethno-mercenarism. This article investigates the historical, ecological, and political drivers underlying this mode of armed mobilization, distinguishing it from prior models of mercenarism and militia politics. Relying on first-hand field observations, institutional analysis, relevant literature, and a newly proposed gametheoretic framework, the study explores how clan networks, external patronage, and environmental pressures coalesce to produce robust, mobile, and market-driven armed groups. The implications for policy and international intervention are discussed.

title: Chad’s Accession to the Arab League in Light of Egyptian–Chadian Relations
affiliations: Cairo University

detail.title: Chad’s Accession to the Arab League in Light of Egyptian–Chadian Relations
detail.abstract:
This paper,  explores the prospects and implications of Chad’s accession to the Arab League within the broader framework of Egyptian–Chadian relations. The study begins by outlining the historical, geographic, and cultural ties between Egypt and Chad, emphasizing Chad’s strategic importance as a bridge between the Arab world and sub-Saharan Africa. It then examines the evolution of bilateral relations in political, economic, and cultural fields, highlighting cooperation in agriculture, health, education, and infrastructure, with Egyptian firms such as Arab Contractors playing a major role.

The paper reviews regional dynamics and the rationale behind the proposal—first discussed during the 2010 Arab League Summit—to admit Chad as a full member, given that Arabic is an official language in its constitution and that the country shares deep historical and cultural connections with Arab nations.

In its recommendations, the study argues that Chad’s accession would strengthen Arab–African integration, enhance Egypt’s strategic and economic influence in Central Africa, and support mutual development. It calls for expanding Arabic language education in Chad, establishing joint investment and friendship associations, and considering future Egyptian economic and even security cooperation frameworks in Chad. Ultimately, the paper concludes that closer Egypt–Chad and Arab–African cooperation would yield significant political and economic benefits for all sides.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the concepts and indices of economic resilience and vulnerability. The central notion in clarifying both resilience and vulnerability is that of an adverse shock. If a shock does not alter the growth path of an economy or cause a recession, the economy is considered "resilient." Resilience refers to an economy's ability to return to its pre-shock growth trajectory. A resilient economy, after experiencing a shock, resumes its long-term growth path. Endogenous growth can strengthen economic resilience, and resilient economies tend to experience sustainable growth. Macroeconomic stability and effective institutions are two principal indicators of economic resilience. Resilience stems largely from economic policymaking, while vulnerability is related to the inherent structural characteristics of an economy that expose it to adverse shocks. Export concentration, dependence on strategic imports and external financing, as well as geographical vulnerability, constitute the main indicators of economic vulnerability. The greater the capacity to respond to shocks, the lower the vulnerability. The paper explores the indices of economic resilience, including Briguglio, Centennial group and Oxford FM Global. In vulnerability indices, the paper discusses the Briguglio vulnerability index, Guillamount and OECD indices.

detail.abstract: This study provides a comparative analysis of electoral integrity, voter participation, and institutional reforms in Southern and West Africa, focusing on South Africa (2024), Lesotho (2022), Malawi (2025), and Ghana (2024). Drawing on election observer mission reports from 2022 to 2025, the study examines trends in voter turnout, gendered participation, youth engagement, and legal-institutional reforms. Despite high registration rates, persistent voter apathy-particularly among youth-and low representation of women in political leadership highlight the gap between procedural compliance and substantive democratic engagement. Observer missions consistently recommend targeted civic education, institutional strengthening, harmonization of electoral laws, digital governance oversight, and inclusive policies to enhance participation and trust. By synthesizing crosscountry lessons, the study underscores the importance of linking electoral integrity to democratic consolidation, demonstrating a pathway "from low turnout to inclusive participation". The findings offer actionable insights for policymakers, electoral commissions, and scholars seeking to strengthen credible, inclusive, and participatory electoral systems in Africa.

title: Copyright, Learnright, and Fair Use: Rethinking Compensation for AI Model Training
affiliations: Cornell University - Law School, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and George Washington University Law Center

detail.title: Copyright, Learnright, and Fair Use: Rethinking Compensation for AI Model Training

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cornell Legal Studies Research Paper No. 25-37
publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Northwestern Journal of Technology and Intellectual Property, Vol. 23, Issue 1

detail.abstract:
Generative AI can rapidly output vast amounts of expressive content, some of which has great value for society. This new computational process also raises a deep question of fairness: Will the original creators of the content used to train these systems share in the value they create? The question becomes particularly urgent as the potential effects of generative AI on markets for creative works become clearer. Artists with a distinctive style may find it nearly impossible to sell their new work when very low-cost substitutes can be generated automatically. News publishers whose content can now be paraphrased by generative AI systems without violating copyright laws may lose significant advertising revenue from readers who no longer need to click through to publishers’ websites. Millions of workers may be wholly or partially displaced by generative AI trained on their works.

Numerous scholars have begun to address this issue. Some have focused on challenging generative AI providers’ claims that their ingestion of copyrighted works for training models and outputting new works is fair use. Others have conceded or bracketed the fair use question and proposed levies or compulsory licenses to compensate for these uses. We take a distinct approach, proposing a new right for copyright holders with respect to AI training using their work. This protection is appropriate given massive AI systems’ ability to process vast amounts of information far faster and less expensively than humans can. An exclusive right to license AI training, called a “learnright” for short, would enable copyright holders to claim some share in the revenues arising out of automated systems that learn from covered material.

This essay examines the rationale and potential mechanisms for implementing such laws. It explains the high degree of legal uncertainty surrounding the many current lawsuits against generative AI providers, and it proposes learnrights to complement the existing exclusive rights guaranteed to copyright holders. Given the many sources from which AI can “learn,” market mechanisms would likely permit a fair and reasonable degree of revenue sharing pursuant to copyright holders’ assertion of their learnrights. Compensation for learnrights would also redress some striking imbalances apparent in current copyright policy that favor mechanical processing of texts over human engagement with them.

detail.abstract: Supply chains transmit information before markets price it. Customer performance reveals emerging demand, and supplier performance reveals capacity and execution risk. These directional spillovers move through networks in predictable ways. When customers are getting stronger, suppliers see order flow and revenue visibility improve. When suppliers are stable and delivering reliably, customers maintain margins and avoid operational bottlenecks. Both channels matter. When both directions turn positive at the same time, the effect compounds: companies benefit from improving demand and a supply base capable of supporting it.

title: Marriage Increases Women's Unpaid Care Work by 44%, Men's Unchanged: Evidence from India
affiliations: Apna.Co

detail.title: Marriage Increases Women's Unpaid Care Work by 44%, Men's Unchanged: Evidence from India
detail.abstract: Using India's 2024 Time Use Survey (10.2 million observations, 139,489 households), we document a stark marriage penalty in unpaid care work: marriage increases women's care work participation by 2.1 percentage points (44% increase) while having zero effect on men's participation. This penalty is 2.4 times larger for younger women (25) than older women (>25), and persists across all education levels, urban-rural locations, and employment status. We find no gender difference in time intensity conditional on participation, indicating the disparity operates entirely on the participation margin. These findings reveal marriage as a critical institution activating gender-specific norms about domestic responsibilities, with important implications for policies targeting gender equality in household production.

title: Managing Democracy in a Fragile Political Landscape: Assessing the Capacity of Lesotho’s Electoral Commission to Foster Integrity, Inclusivity, and Public Trust

detail.title: Managing Democracy in a Fragile Political Landscape: Assessing the Capacity of Lesotho’s Electoral Commission to Foster Integrity, Inclusivity, and Public Trust
detail.abstract: The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) of Lesotho has administered national elections since 1997 in a fragile political environment characterized by recurring coalition instability, contested processes, and declining public confidence. The 2022 General Elections, marked by the country's lowest-ever voter turnout at 37.7 percent, highlighted persistent structural challenges in electoral governance. Allegations of inaccuracies in the voter register and the underrepresentation of youth raised concerns about electoral integrity. The late adjustment of constituency boundaries further undermined public trust. Barriers faced by women and persons with disabilities revealed critical shortcomings in inclusivity and equitable participation. This paper critically assesses the IEC's capacity to foster integrity, inclusivity, and public trust within such a volatile context. Drawing on electoral data, observer reports, and the legal framework, the analysis demonstrates that while the Commission broadly complies with its statutory mandate, systemic weaknesses in voter registration, civic and voter education, and inter-agency coordination continue to erode legitimacy. To address these gaps, two reform priorities are emphasized. First, the institutionalization of robust and continuous civic and voter education, particularly targeting youth, women, and marginalized groups. Second, the enhancement of the voter register's accuracy and inclusiveness through sustained cross-institutional collaboration. By situating the Lesotho case within broader debates on democratic resilience, the paper highlights the dual role of election management bodies as both technical administrators and guardians of democratic legitimacy in fragile political landscapes.

title: Breaking the Low-Level Equilibrium: A Two-sided Approach to Household Waste Segregation in Bangladesh
affiliations: Bennett University and Wageningen University and Research (WUR) - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Breaking the Low-Level Equilibrium: A Two-sided Approach to Household Waste Segregation in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Developing countries are often trapped in a low-level equilibrium in waste segregation, where households and waste collectors lack sufficient incentives to alter their practices. In this study, we examine a combined intervention approach from both the household side and the collection side. Specifically, we conducted an experiment in Mymensingh, Bangladesh with three treatment conditions: (1) information only, (2) information plus a bucket, and (3) information plus plastic bags—all alongside a segregated collection service. We find that an intervention that combines a one-time information campaign with a segregated collection service can increase the household waste segregation rate by 30 percentage points. Supplementing information provision with either buckets or plastic bags can further improve waste segregation. Furthermore, we show that the improved household waste segregation benefits the downstream waste processing plant. Our results demonstrate that policies integrating collection-side and household-side interventions could initiate a transition toward sustainable waste management in developing countries.

title: The Role of Persistent Climate-Driven Financial Effects in Estimating Climate Damages through Integrated Assessment Models

This work used resources of the Deutsches Klimarechenzentrum (DKRZ) granted by its Scientific Steering Committee (WLA) under project IDs 0033 and 1275.

detail.abstract: Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) are essential for analyzing the long-term economic consequences of climate change, yet their climate damage functions remain a primary source of uncertainty and critique. Current e[orts focus on disaggregating immediate biophysical impacts, often overlooking or simplifying financial feedback loops. This paper introduces a novel, climate-driven financial damage channel into a new IAM, FRIDA v2.1, specifically focusing on the relationship between climate change and increased nonperforming loans. We characterize this financial damage as a time-dependent, inertial e[ect, impairing the financial sector's ability to support investments in the long term. The results demonstrate that incorporating this persistent financial channel leads to significantly higher estimates of long-term economic damage compared to DICE style aggregate climate damage functions. These findings underscore the necessity for IAMs to explicitly model persistent, climate-driven financial feedback mechanisms to accurately capture long-term climate risk and provide robust guidance for mitigation policy.

title: Overlapping Community Detection in Mixed Membership Vector Autoregression

detail.title: Overlapping Community Detection in Mixed Membership Vector Autoregression
detail.abstract: In this work, we introduce a novel cluster affiliation vector autoregressive model, termed the mixed membership stochastic block vector autoregression (MMSB-VAR(p)). This model assumes that the VAR coefficients at all lags are random matrices following a joint distribution defined by a probabilistic generative framework. The panel data generated by this model can exhibit either single or multiple membership structures with the estimated VAR coefficients recovering the corresponding non-overlapping or overlapping block structures. To uncover the latent group structure, we propose a two-step algorithm leveraging the key insight that spillover effects within groups are significantly stronger than those between groups. We establish the consistency of the proposed algorithm and the simulation study demonstrates its effectiveness. Finally, we apply our methodology to analyze public opinions about the Ukraine-Russia war on Reddit.

detail.title: Political Identity and Consumer Behavior: Musk and Tesla in Germany
detail.abstract: We examine how Elon Musk's public endorsement of Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in December 2024 affected Tesla sales. Using district-level monthly registration data and a difference-indifferences design, we show that new Tesla registrations increased by up to 30% in right-leaning regions but stagnated or declined in left-leaning ones. Event-study estimates indicate no pre-trends but a persistent post-event divergence. The effect does not extend to other electric vehicle brands. The results demonstrate that corporate political influence can polarize consumer demand along partisan lines.

title: Bank Fees and Household Financial Well-Being

detail.title: Bank Fees and Household Financial Well-Being
detail.abstract: Even very straightforward policy changes in the provision of consumer nancial services can fail to impact the vulnerable households they would have been expected to benet. In this study, we examine policy changes from large U.S. banks between 2017 and 2022, which eliminated non-sucient funds (NSF) fees and relaxed overdraft policies. Using individual transaction-level data, we nd that the elimination of NSF fees, not surprisingly, resulted in immediate reductions in NSF charges across the income distribution. However, relaxing overdraft policies resulted in reductions in overdraft fees only for wealthier households, along the dimensions of income and liquidity, and only those enjoyed subsequent declines in late fees, interest payments, account maintenance fees, and the use of alternative nancial services, such as payday loans. Our results thus suggest that the policy changes were not substantial enough to signicantly reduce the nancial stress of the more vulnerable households. Finally, as our setting features multiple treatments and variation in treatment intensities, we theoretically motivate and empirically implement a new stacked event study estimator closely related to de de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2024) to address the biases arising from staggered DID specications.

detail.abstract: Bangladesh's health sector faces persistent and deeply rooted challenges, including weak governance, shortage of skilled workforce, inadequate financing, mismanagement of resources, and poor quality of service delivery. Despite notable improvements in maternal and child health indicators over the past decades, the system continues to experience inefficiencies that undermine progress. This article explores these systemic challenges by applying a management point of view, drawing insights from the works of Khaled (2025), who emphasizes the role of strategic planning, institutional discipline, leadership capability, and organizational efficiency in improving government sectors. In addition to identifying major problems, this paper presents a management-oriented roadmap for sustainable health sector reform in Bangladesh. The recommendations are based on practical experiences, academic research, and lessons from public sector management perspectives. By integrating management principles such as accountability, strategic vision, human resource development, and technological innovation, the article aims to offer a structured, implementable solution for strengthening the health system. The expected outcomes include improved service delivery, enhanced governance structures, efficient resource utilization, and greater trust in public healthcare institutions.

detail.title: Teachers' Perspectives on the Use of AI Detection Tools: Insights from Ridge Regression Analysis
detail.abstract: This study explores the perceptions of 213 Filipino teachers toward AI detection tools in academic settings. It focuses on the factors that influence teachers' trust, concerns, and decision-making regarding these tools. The research investigates how teachers' trust in AI detection tools affects their perceptions of fairness and decision-making in evaluating student outputs. It also explores how concerns about AI tools and social norms influence the relationship between trust and decision-making. Ridge Regression analysis was used to examine the relationships between the predictors and the dependent variable. The results revealed that trust in AI detection tools is the most significant predictor of perceived fairness and decision-making among teachers. Concerns about AI tools and social norms have weaker effects on teachers' perceptions. The study emphasized critical role of trust in shaping teachers' perceptions of AI detection tools. Teachers who trust these tools are more likely to view them as fair and effective. In contrast, concerns and social norms have a limited influence on perceptions and decisionmaking. For recommendations, training and institutional guidelines should emphasize how these tools work, their limitations, and best practices for their use. Striking a balance between policy enforcement and educator support is essential for fostering trust in AI detection technologies. Encouraging experienced users to share insights through communities of practice could enhance the adoption and effective use of AI detection tools in educational settings.

We develop the PartiaCorr-mixed-SCORE algorithm to estimate mixed memberships under the 2PPCN structure. We establish the consistency of the proposed method and demonstrate its effectiveness in simulated study. Finally, we apply our approach to U.S. state-level employment growth data to uncover latent industry-based mixed membership structures across states in U.S.

detail.abstract: The accelerating climate and biodiversity crises demand solutions that are sustainable, inclusive, and equitable. Gender, shaping vulnerabilities, capacities, and decision power, fundamentally determines how communities experience environmental risks and mobilize responses. Women and gender diverse people lead as decision makers, resource stewards, scientists, and activists, yet face persistent barriers to access, participation, recognition, and safety across environmental sectors. detail.abstract: We estimate and compare impacts of cash and in-kind transfers on the consumption of temptation goods in the same population, and explore normative implications. We use two decades of data from South Carolina on cash benefits from Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and in-kind benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) linked to detailed data on adults' health care use. Our empirical strategy examines outcome changes in the several days following each transfer's scheduled monthly payout. Emergency department visits for drug and alcohol use increase by 20-30 percent following SSI receipt, but do not respond to SNAP receipt. Fills of prescription drugs for new illnesses also increase following SSI receipt but do not respond to SNAP receipt. Motivated by these non-fungibility results, we develop a model of a paternalistic social planner choosing the mix of cash and SNAP for a fixed-budget transfer program when consumers have self-control problems and may engage in mental accounting. We show that the planner's optimal SNAP share is strictly positive and weakly increasing as self-control worsens. Moreover, with heterogeneity in self-control and mental accounting, the planner may choose to use SNAP even when they have access to a uniform Pigouvian tax on the temptation good.

detail.abstract: Anxiety about falling behind can drive people to embrace emerging technologies with uncertain consequences. We study how social forces shape demand for AI-based learning tools early in the education pipeline. In incentivized experiments with parents-key gatekeepers for children's AI adoption-we elicit their demand for unrestricted AI tools for teenagers' education. Parental demand rises with the share of other teenagers using the technology, with social forces increasing willingness to pay for AI by more than 60%. Providing information about potentially adverse effects of unstructured AI use negatively shifts beliefs about the merits of AI, but does not change individual demand. Instead, this information increases parents' preference for banning AI in schools. Follow-up experiments show that social information has little effect on beliefs about AI quality, perceived skill priorities, or support for bans, suggesting that effects operate through social pressure rather than social learning. Our evidence highlights social pressure driving individual technology adoption despite widespread support for restricting its use.

detail.abstract: We explore the macroeconomic effects of climate policies promoting the green energy transition in the euro area using an extended version of the Euro Area and Global Economy (EAGLE) model. The model differentiates between brown and green energy sectors and incorporates carbon taxes and brown capital income taxes. We analyze scenarios with unilateral and globally coordinated carbon taxes, with and without revenue redistribution to green firms and financially constrained households. Carbon taxes act as negative supply shocks, raising inflation and lowering output, while subsidies to green energy firms reduce green energy prices, supporting the transition and easing recessions. Redistribution to constrained households boosts consumption but does not accelerate the green transition. Taxes on brown capital income lower both inflation and output by acting as demand shocks. Recycling revenue from this tax to subsidize green capital investment strengthens the shift to green energy and moderates economic contractions. Global coordination of carbon taxes delivers only modest additional macroeconomic effects compared with unilateral action, as substitution in energy use outweighs international spillovers. Sensitivity analyses confirm the robustness of these findings under alternative assumptions about price rigidity, substitution elasticities and monetary policy.

detail.title: From Symmetry-Breaking to Causality: A Definite Framework for Causal Inference *
detail.abstract: The core impediment to causal inference lies in a profound symmetry. In the foundational model Y = X + e, the causal direction between X and Y becomes statistically unidentifiable when both terms are normally distributed, creating a long-standing philosophical and technical stalemate. This paper presents a resolution by moving from symmetry to asymmetry. We introduce a novel framework that, through an asymmetric transformation based on Generalized Measures of Correlation (GMC), establishes a definite causal link. This approach provides, for the first time, a necessary and sufficient condition to ascertain the direction from X to Y , resolving the identifiability problem at its most elementary level. Moreover, we prove that this inference is not merely definite, but also optimal under the Minimum Mean Squared Prediction Error (MMSPE) principle. We will present extensive evidence of its superior performance across  diverse fields. Finally, the paper will explore how this framework facilitates causal discovery in large and high dimension datasets and points toward a new type causal relationship, inviting a fresh philosophical examination of causality itself.

title: The Entropy of Excellence

detail.title: The Entropy of Excellence
detail.abstract: This paper presents the Unified Operating Model (UOM), integrating Robert Simons' research on entrepreneurial gaps with Moral Tipping Point (MTP) Theory to create a comprehensive framework for organizational pressure management. The core insight is that pressure is an amplifier, not a driver; what matters is what exists beneath it. The model establishes that ethical and operational failures divide into distinct categories requiring different interventions: functional duress-driven failures respond to enablement, identity duress-driven failures respond to signal architecture, and opportunism-driven failures respond to scrutiny. Organizations struggle when they misallocate these levers. This revised edition integrates Signal Architecture as a fourth intervention lever, adds Gate 0 (Identity Duress Risk Assessment) to the implementation sequence, and provides explicit treatment of interaction effects between failure modes.

title: The Drowning Curve

detail.title: The Drowning Curve
detail.abstract: Moral Tipping Point Theory (MTP) provides a mathematical and behavioral framework for understanding why people fail ethically and what interventions actually work. The core insight is that ethical failure has two fundamentally different modes, opportunism-driven and duress-driven, and each requires a different organizational response. This revised edition introduces a key refinement: duress itself divides into two subtypes with different saturation properties and intervention requirements. Functional Duress (D f) arises from external pressure and responds to enablement. Identity Duress (D i) arises from threat to perceived competence and responds to signal architecture: changing what an action means rather than how hard it is. Many organizations treat all failure as an observation problem: "If we tracked it better, people would behave." This is true for opportunism-driven failure, where surveillance raises the cost of taking. It is largely ineffective for duress-driven failure, where surveillance adds stress without reducing the underlying friction that causes the failure.

detail.abstract: Urged by the European Energy Crisis and the threatening consequences of severe natural gas shortages, energy providers launched gas-saving initiatives incorporating financial incentives to reduce residential natural gas consumption. In collaboration with one of Germany's largest energy providers, we conducted a natural field experiment (N = 2,598) to evaluate the effectiveness of a behaviorally-guided co-design of such a gas-saving initiative by implementing two established behavioral instruments-reminders of gas saving intentions and descriptive norm feedback. Our findings show limited effectiveness of the behavioral instruments during the high-price period. The feedback risks a "boomerang effect" among households with above-average initial savings, who reduce their conservation efforts in response. The reminder does not significantly enhance savings in our main specifications, yet, realizes 1 percentage point savings in alternate models refining for outliers. Potential mechanisms include a significant intentionaction gap and misperceived effectiveness of energy-saving actions, which are not alleviated by the reminder.

detail.abstract: We study a mechanism-design problem in which spiteful agents strive to not only maximize their rewards but also, contingent upon their own payoff levels, seek to lower the opponents' rewards. We characterize all individually rational (IR) and incentivecompatible (IC) mechanisms that are immune to such spiteful behavior, showing that they take the form of threshold mechanisms with an ordering of the agents. Building on this characterization, we prove two impossibility results: under either anonymity or efficiency, any such IR and IC mechanism collapses to the null mechanism, which never allocates the item to any agent. Leveraging these findings, we partially extend our analysis to a multi-item setup. These results illuminate the challenges of auctioning items in the natural presence of other-regarding preferences.

detail.abstract: We propose a general and simple deep learning extension of Statistical Jump Models in the spirit of a Mixture-of-Experts framework. This framework is designed to ensemble neural networks via inferred latent state distributions. We detail the variants and applications of Deep Statistical Jump Models such as regime-switching factor models, end-to-end decision models, among others. We also describe how to use Block Coordinate Gradient Descent to fit this type of models and discuss practical implementation details. As part of the fitting algorithm and in order to obtain probability estimates in the state inference step, we propose a smoothed relaxation of standard Viterbi algorithm for structured state inference from discrete state labels to the probability simplex. We also apply existing theoretical framework to show convergence of the fitting algorithm and quantify the error introduced by the smoothed dynamic programming. We demonstrate the framework on synthetic data generated from a Hidden Markov Model with quadratic factor emissions and compare against classical Statistical Jump Models and disjoint modeling baselines in both supervised and unsupervised settings.

detail.title: Labour History and the Economics of Natural Resources
detail.abstract: Labour was traditionally at the centre of historical and sociological studies of natural resource extraction. This is no longer the case as the size, visibility and collective organisation of workforces in the extractive industries - all of which captured scholarly attention - has declined. This chapter takes a long-term and global perspective on the history of labour and natural resource extraction from the early nineteenth century to the present. It identifies and described two major trends in the extractive industries: The first is the relative decline in the numbers working in extractive industries even as output has increased enormously. The second is that the racial and gender hierarchies that determined who could do what job have slowly been dismantled. Hierarchies of gender and race hardened and spread during the nineteenth century to become commonplace features of the industry.

title: Citywide Orchestration of Electric Vehicle Battery Swapping

detail.title: Citywide Orchestration of Electric Vehicle Battery Swapping
detail.abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) battery swapping has been thriving, particularly in the electric ride-hailing sector; yet, operational innovation lags behind this market expansion. Current practices often adhere to rigid strategies like uniform battery stock allocation, causing severe spatial mismatches between demand and available batteries. Resolving this from the supply side proves intractable: on one hand, further increasing battery inventory is financially and environmentally prohibitive; on the other hand, repositioning bulky batteries is logistically formidable. To circumvent this impasse, we investigate a demand-side breakthrough: coordinated swapping. This innovation aligns demand with supply by proactively guiding vehicles to designated stations. This paper examines the fundamental challenges of designing a swapping station network to enable this coordination and evaluating its efficiency. Specifically, we model station operations using stochastic inventory theory and propose a two-stage distributionally robust optimization model for joint location and capacity planning. This model presents challenges due to bilinear terms and sums of piecewise linear functions in the second-stage problem. Notably, we prove the convexity of the second-stage problem and reveal a distinctive structure in its dual solution. These model properties guide us in designing efficient column-and-constraint generation algorithms. We also propose two alternative strategies and extend persistence theory in discrete optimization to reformulate them as mixed-integer second-order cone programs. We validate the efficacy of our algorithms and the performance of our proposed strategies using real transportation data from Beijing. Results indicate that coordinated swapping excels in managing spatial demand distribution due to its flexibility. These benefits amplify with lower service rates and higher grid capacity. Furthermore, enhanced grid capacity results in a spatially heterogeneous battery distribution, and ongoing technological advancements give rise to a U-shaped pattern in battery inventory size. In a broader context, this work illuminates the role of mobility-energy coordination in enabling smart cities.

detail.abstract: This study examines the ethical challenges posed by algorithmic bias in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its implications for governance, fairness, and accountability. As AI becomes more integrated into daily life and organizational decision-making, unintentional biases from data, model design, and implementation can undermine fairness and trust. Such biases contribute to inequitable outcomes in areas like hiring, healthcare, and analytics, raising serious legal and societal concerns. The paper highlights the need for robust AI governance frameworks, including regulatory oversight, audit mechanisms, and explainable systems, to ensure accountability. Ultimately, it argues that mitigating algorithmic bias is vital for fostering responsible, transparent, and socially beneficial AI development.

title: Volatility, Skewness Spill-overs and the Role of News Surprises: Dynamics in Foreign Exchange Markets

detail.title: Volatility, Skewness Spill-overs and the Role of News Surprises: Dynamics in Foreign Exchange Markets
detail.abstract: This study analyses volatility and skewness spill-overs in G7, Australian, New Zealand, and Chinese currency option markets by employing a VAR framework to capture dynamic linkages between news announcement surprises, implied volatility, and skewness across five regimes: the Global Financial Crisis, European Sovereign Debt Crisis, Covid-19 Crisis, precrisis economic growth, and monetary policy normalisation. The results reveal persistent volatility spill-overs, with CAD and EUR as central risk transmitters, while CNY remains largely insulated except during periods of extreme market stress. News surprises exert limited influence except during precrisis expansion, and skewness spill-overs display regime-dependent patterns. These findings highlight the importance of regime-based policy responses and strengthened international coordination.

detail.abstract: Measuring inequality in West Africa is a challenging task that is constrained by the limited availability and irregular collection of household consumption data. To address this challenge, we reconstructed the evolution of inequality in the Sahel region using an innovative framework that combines Survey-to-Survey Imputation Techniques (SSITs) with Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS), based on labour force surveys conducted in eight countries between 2003 and 2021. The findings highlight pronounced regional disparities, persistent levels of inequality, and a clear association between inequality patterns and episodes of conflict or political instability. Our contribution is twofold: methodologically, we introduce a flexible SSIT-GAMLSS model that incorporates two levels of random effects; substantively, we provide new evidence of inequality trends in francophone West Africa, a region largely underrepresented in empirical research.

detail.title: Operational Metrics in Derivatives Adoption: Evidence from China’s Chemical Industry
detail.abstract: This study examines the role of financial derivatives in managing operational and financial risks within China's chemical manufacturing sector. While prior research has primarily focused on financial determinants of hedging decisions, we highlight the significant influence of operational metrics—particularly inventory levels and turnover rates—in shaping firms’ engagement in derivatives markets. Drawing from a sample of 289 publicly listed chemical firms from 2016 to 2022, we employ probit regression and K-means clustering to explore how operational and financial factors jointly determine derivatives adoption.Our empirical results reveal that operational metrics have a non-negligible impact on hedging decisions. Specifically, inventory and turnover rates emerge as primary determinants of firms' initiatives, while pre-tax operating profit remains significant from a financial perspective. The moderation analysis of cash flow reveals that financially constrained firms prioritize derivatives for operational risk mitigation, while resource-abundant firms employ them selectively for strategic optimization. Furthermore, our robustness tests, which control for geographical distinctions and the COVID-19 effect, confirm that firm-specific operational characteristics consistently dominate firms' hedging decisions despite regional heterogeneity. Finally, clustering analysis underscores the interplay between operational efficiency and capital robustness, showing that firms exhibiting superior operational efficiency and capital robustness demonstrate higher engagement in derivatives hedging. These findings contribute to the corporate risk management literature by expounding on the primacy of operational considerations in derivatives usage, particularly in asset-intensive industries. The study also provides practical implications for manufacturing firms navigating volatile market conditions, emphasizing that integrating operational and financial strategies is crucial for effective risk management.

title: Optimizers and Satisfiers: A Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) of the Use of Character Strengths in Brazilian Professionals and Associations with Engagement, Life Satisfaction, and Burnout

detail.title: Optimizers and Satisfiers: A Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) of the Use of Character Strengths in Brazilian Professionals and Associations with Engagement, Life Satisfaction, and Burnout
detail.abstract: Character strengths are key positive traits vital for human flourishing, but overuse or underuse can harm well-being. This study validated the Overuse-Underuse-Optimal Use (OUOU) Scale in Brazil and explored links with work engagement, life satisfaction, and burnout among 457 Brazilian professionals. Traditional psychometric methods, such as confirmatory factor analyses, produced poor model fit. Hartigan’s dip test showed significant multimodality in all variables, indicating hidden population differences that break assumptions of factor analysis. As a result, latent profile analysis (LPA) was used, revealing a strong two-group solution that distinguished "optimizers," who show balanced strength use, from "satisficers," who display less optimal patterns, in a 1:3 ratio. Structural equation modeling found that being an optimizer predicted higher life satisfaction, more work engagement, and increased job crafting behaviors. It also predicted lower burnout, including exhaustion, mental distance, cognitive impairment, and emotional impairment. Furthermore, virtue-specific LPA uncovered diverse overuse-underuse patterns across the six VIA virtues. These results suggest that most people tend to satisfice in their strength use, pointing to opportunities for interventions that encourage optimizing. The study highlights the importance of person-centered approaches when traditional measures based on continua violate key psychometric assumptions.

title: Feedback on ECHA’s Proposal for a Basic Regulation

detail.title: Feedback on ECHA’s Proposal for a Basic Regulation
detail.abstract: The European Commission’s proposal to establish a standalone regulation for the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) represents a shift in how the EU governs chemical risk. The proposal formalizes ECHA’s mandate outside of its previous anchoring in REACH and recognizes ECHA’s increased scope of work on risk evaluation, cosmetic assessment, and coordination with other EU agencies and bodies. The reform also strengthens core scientific committees, such as the Risk Assessment Committee (RAC), the Socio-Economic Analysis Committee (SEAC), and the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS), in order to accelerate review processes and anticipate higher workloads for biotechnological and chemical review.While the reform is primarily administrative concerning the expansion of scientific review committees and harmonization of chemical assessments, the proposal’s long-term outcomes will ultimately depend on whether it is understood beyond niche groups of regulatory experts. The general public might lack understanding of the scientific models underpinning the proposal’s risk governance, like non-animal testing models (NAMs) and occupational exposure limits (OELs). Without accessible explanations of what the regulation does, the reform might not translate into real public trust. This can solidify into misinformation, panic cycles, or simplistic narratives that miss ECHA’s actual evidence-based approach.This paper examines the proposal from the standpoint of scientific literacy, particularly concerning the regulation’s public reception for young researchers. We argue that reforms to ECHA’s internal governance must be accompanied by public-facing communication in order to foster trust, equitable access to information, and a future workplace capable of engaging responsibly with chemical innovation and biotechnology.

detail.abstract: Traditional Learning and Development (L&D) models frequently fail to deliver strategically aligned outcomes due to their reliance on disciplinary silos, often lacking integration between business context, instructional rigor, and psychological insight. Drawing on the Resource-Based View (RBV) of the firm and Strategic Human Resource Development (SHRD) literature, this paper argues that optimal L&D effectiveness requires an interdisciplinary synthesis of expertise. We propose the Interdisciplinary L&D Model, which mandates the integration of three strategic roles: the Strategic Architect (aligned with business strategy), the Master Instructor (grounded in pedagogical rigor and competency-based training), and the Resilience Coach (focused on performance psychology and growth mindset). This model addresses the full spectrum of development: the Relevance (the Why), the Effectiveness (the How), and the Sustainability (the Will).  The Nads.Talk L&D Service provides an illustrative case, demonstrating how a diverse, integrated professional background can operationalize this framework. The paper concludes by discussing the model's implications for developing T-shaped L&D professionals and suggests future quantitative research to empirically validate the link between interdisciplinary L&D and enhanced organizational resilience.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between internationalization strategy and corporate innovation, and the moderating role of interlocking board networks, using data from Chinese manufacturing firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges between 2009 and 2019. Our findings reveal a significant positive relationship between internationalization strategy, as measured by relative overseas sales, and corporate innovation, as measured by R&D investments and patents. We also find that interlocking board networks positively moderate this relationship, strengthening the link between internationalization and innovation. These results remain robust after a series of tests employing alternative measures of internationalization and innovation and controlling for potential endogeneity and sample selection bias. We also find that the positive relationship between internationalization and innovation remains significant for Chinese manufacturing firms with exclusive OFDI in less-developed economies, which suggests reverse technology spillovers are not the primary driver of the relationship.

title: The Equity Risk Premium as Intentional Emergence: Micro-Idiosyncratic Risk Theory (MIRT)

detail.title: The Equity Risk Premium as Intentional Emergence: Micro-Idiosyncratic Risk Theory (MIRT)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Undergraduate at Hanken School of Economics in Helsinki.
declarations.funderStatement: Independent research.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Micro-Idiosyncratic Risk Theory (MIRT), which argues that strategic intentions under uncertainty are the primary controllable source of ex ante equity risk. These micro-intentions aggregate upward through industry linkages, shared heuristics, and institutional amplification-via index funds, volatility targeting, and analyst herding-producing the co-movement captured by beta and factor models.

At the macro level, these aggregated uncertainties stabilize into a coordination equilibrium: the Equity Risk Premium (ERP). Rather than a structural constant, the ERP acts as a focal point that aligns expectations across market participants and feeds back downward by shaping firms' cost of capital. Exogenous shocks still matter, but in MIRT their impact is mediated and amplified through intentional responses and institutional channels.

MIRT offers a causal explanation for beta instability, factor regime shifts, and ERP persistence. A simple agent-based simulation demonstrates that a realistic ERP, noisy but meaningful betas, and strong intention-outcome coupling can emerge without ex ante covariance assumptions. The theory yields testable predictions, including that intention-based variables should outperform beta in explaining implied discount rates, that the ERP should have limited explanatory power for firm-level risk, and that beta stability should rise with passive ownership intensity.

title: An Alternative Economic Model for Non-Rival Goods in the Digital Age: Aligned Incentives for Sustainable Success and Collective Value

detail.title: An Alternative Economic Model for Non-Rival Goods in the Digital Age: Aligned Incentives for Sustainable Success and Collective Value
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of an alternative economic model for nonrival goods in the digital economy, examining how cost-sharing mechanisms can simultaneously improve creator success probability while democratizing access to digital goods. The proposed model reconceptualizes pricing as Revenue /Q=P , where costs are distributed among users, creating a unique incentive structure that transforms passive consumers into active recruiters. Drawing upon theoretical advances in auction mechanisms [1], anti-rival good theory [2], and empirical evidence from digital platforms [3], this study demonstrates how the model addresses two critical failures in digital markets: the 99% creator failure rate in winner-take-all economies and the artificial scarcity that limits access to non-rival goods. Through game-theoretic analysis, we show how aligning user incentives with creator success creates self-reinforcing growth dynamics that can make otherwise unviable projects sustainable. The model offers a rational risk-management strategy for creators-trading lottery-ticket economics for higher-probability sustainable income-while simultaneously serving communities through transparent, participatory economics. Analysis of platform cooperatives, open source projects, and emerging blockchain implementations reveals design principles for practical application. We propose concrete implementation pathways, including highvisibility cultural events that could demonstrate viability. The paper contributes to digital economics literature by showing how self-interest and collective benefit can be aligned through mechanism design, offering creators a pragmatic alternative that improves their odds of success while expanding access to digital goods.

title: Setting Boundaries and Standards in Transportation: Between Principles of Sufficientarianism and Limitarianism
affiliations: University of Toronto and Human Geography and Spatial Planning Department

detail.title: Setting Boundaries and Standards in Transportation: Between Principles of Sufficientarianism and Limitarianism
detail.abstract:
This article offers a conceptual and critical contribution to the transport literature by bringing together two ethical principles, sufficientarianism and limitarianism, to advance a justice-oriented rethinking of mobility systems. Discussions of sufficiency have increasingly informed debates on minimum standards of accessibility and basic mobility rights, particularly in relation to social exclusion and inequitable access. However, the complementary notion of limitarianism, the moral case for upper limits on excessive consumption, remains largely absent from transport policy discourse. We argue that the failure to address both extremes simultaneously obscures the inherently political and distributive nature of mobility, allowing patterns of hypermobility and resource-intensive travel by privileged groups to persist at the expense of marginalized populations and ecological systems.

Drawing from transportation, environmental, political philosophy, economic and sustainability scholarship, we engage with frameworks that conceptualize both floors and ceilings of provision, including Raworth’s Doughnut Economics, Gough’s sustainable welfare model, and debates on planetary boundaries. We propose that transport systems should be governed within a clearly defined normative corridor: guaranteeing sufficient, dignified, and meaningful access for all, while curbing excessive and environmentally harmful forms of mobility that undermine collective well-being and equity. 

The paper develops this argument in four stages. First, we examine the ethical foundations of sufficientarianism and limitarianism and their relevance to transport. Second, we critically review literature addressing boundaries, standards, and limits across disciplines and synthesize its implications for transport policy and planning. Third, we offer a framework and preliminary guidelines for defining and operationalizing lower and upper thresholds of access and mobility. Fourth, we illustrate how these ideas might be applied through examples from transport and mobility research, many of which align with these principles in spirit, though not yet explicitly connected to them.

By combining features of narrative and critical review, this paper seeks to reposition transport not merely as a technical system but as a moral and political domain where questions of who moves, how much, at what cost, and with what environmental consequences must be central. We argue that integrating sufficientarian and limitarian perspectives provides a powerful lens for advancing socially equitable and environmentally responsible transport futures, supporting a more explicit normative foundation for policies aimed at achieving transport equity within planetary boundaries.

detail.abstract: This research examines Green Service Quality (GSQ) as a key factor in increasing tourist satisfaction and the competitiveness of sustainable tourism destinations in Indonesia. GSQ encompasses tangibility, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy, with a strong emphasis on sustainability. The main dimensions of GSQ identified include hotel eco-centricity, staff attitudes towards sustainability, facility quality, location, service character, perceived value, and intention to revisit. The method used is qualitative research with a literature review technique. The findings show that the dimensions of tangibility, reliability, responsiveness, and empathy have a significant effect on visit intention and tourist satisfaction, while assurance tends to be insignificant in some segments, especially Generation Z. Visible and well-functioning GSQ practices become a factor of delight that exceeds basic service expectations, strengthens the guest experience, and supports sustainable tourism development goals. The integration of GSQ into hotel operational strategies through green facility design, environmentally friendly standard procedures, staff training, and certification mechanisms can increase tourist satisfaction, loyalty, and recommendation intentions.

detail.title: Exchange Rate Pass-Through in South Africa: Implications to Sectoral Inflation Expectations
detail.abstract: Exchange rate fluctuations in South Africa, including a 184.60% depreciation of the U.S. dollar, and their pass-through (ERPT) to sectoral inflation expectations remain poorly understood. Existing studies focus on aggregate inflation and assume linear, symmetric effects, limiting policymakers’ insight into sector-specific responses. This study incorporates Markov-switching regimes to capture state-dependent ERPT across financial, business, and trade-union sectors, using quarterly data from 2000Q1 to 2025Q3. We apply NARDL, Markov-switching dynamic regression, and TVP-VAR models to account for nonlinearities, asymmetries, and regime-dependent dynamics. Results reveal sectoral heterogeneity: ERPT is highest in the business sector, moderate in the financial sector, and negative for trade unions. Pass-through is muted in stable regimes but intensifies sharply under high-volatility, weak-rand conditions, particularly for unions, indicating potential wage-price spiral risks. Findings underscore the need for sector-sensitive, regime-aware monetary policy to stabilize expectations and reduce structural vulnerabilities in South Africa.

detail.abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders affect more than 1.3 billion individuals globally, creating substantial clinical and economic burdens. Traditional orthopedic physiotherapy approaches often lack precision, demonstrating considerable inter-therapist variability and suboptimal personalization. This study examines the emerging paradigm of artificial intelligence-driven precision physiotherapy, integrating multimodal machine-learning systems for early diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and individualized rehabilitation protocols. We synthesized current evidence from diagnostic imaging analyses, wearable sensor technologies, predictive analytics, and rehabilitation robotics to evaluate clinical efficacy and implementation feasibility. Findings demonstrate that AI-assisted fracture detection achieves 91.43% sensitivity and 92.12% specificity across diverse anatomical regions, with hand and wrist fractures showing highest performance at 95% sensitivity. Deep learning reconstruction of knee MRI reduced scan times by approximately 45% while maintaining diagnostic equivalence. AI-guided personalized rehabilitation interventions yielded 28% reduction in recovery time, 68% improvement in functional outcomes, and 85% patient adherence rates compared to conventional protocols (12%, 45%, and 62% respectively). Wearable sensor integration with machine learning algorithms enabled realtime exercise monitoring with 98.9% recognition accuracy. Critically, this advancement requires addressing data standardization challenges, algorithm transparency requirements, integration with clinical workflows, and equitable access considerations. This paper demonstrates that precision physiotherapy powered by multimodal AI represents a transformative advancement in rehabilitation science, offering clinician-supported personalized interventions that enhance patient outcomes while maintaining therapeutic professional oversight. Implementation success depends on systematic validation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and thoughtful integration preserving the human dimensions of rehabilitation care.

detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the influence of system quality, ease of use, and data security in technology-based tax systems (Coretax) on tax transparency among tax consulting firms in the Greater Jakarta area (Jabodetabek). As digital transformation continues to reshape public administration, understanding the role of technological features in enhancing transparency is critical. A quantitative research approach was employed, using a structured questionnaire distributed to tax consultants operating within the Jabodetabek region. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with Smart-PLS software to assess the relationship between the independent variables (system quality, ease of use, and data security) and the dependent variable (tax transparency). The findings reveal that system quality and ease of use significantly influence tax transparency, suggesting that user-friendly and efficient systems foster clearer reporting and trust. Additionally, data security contributes positively by reinforcing taxpayer confidence in using Coretax platforms. These results emphasize the importance of enhancing system reliability, simplifying user interfaces, and strengthening data protection measures to optimize transparency in tax administration. The study offers valuable insights for policymakers and tax consulting firms seeking to improve accountability and public trust through digital tax platforms.

detail.abstract:
This article explores the role of artificial intelligence (AI) tools as negotiation and mediation coaches.  Drawing on research from negotiation, mediation, and consumer behavior, the article explains why bots can sometimes coach more effectively than humans.  In this role, they offer on-demand, judgment-free support that can help users prepare strategically and reflect honestly.  This support is especially valuable when seeking help from a human would feel too risky or awkward. 

The article cautions against use of AI for roles requiring emotional intelligence, discretion, or legitimacy, such as negotiators, mediators, or arbitrators.  The article distinguishes between AI as a thinking partner and AI as a decision-maker.  It warns about use of AI tools to replace humans in core dispute resolution roles, though they can significantly enhance human performance as coaches.

detail.abstract: We study how students adjust their early career choices in response to economic crises and how these decisions affect their long-run labor market outcomes. Focusing on Sweden’s deep recession in the early 1990s—which hit the manufacturing and construction sectors hardest—we first show that students whose fathers lost jobs in these sectors were more likely to choose career paths tied to less-affected industries. These students later experienced better labor market outcomes, including higher employment and earnings. Our findings suggest that informational frictions are a key obstacle to structural change and identify career choice as an important channel through which recessions reshape labor markets in the long run.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: A consumer seeking to purchase multiple products may do so at a single store (one-stop shopping) or across multiple stores (multistop shopping). Fixed shopping or search costs rationalize one-stop shopping, which often emerges as the only equilibrium behavior in theoretical models. In reality, however, multistop shopping is common, and evidence suggests that some consumers adopt it to save on expenditures. This paper uses NielsenIQ consumer scanner data to address two questions about multistop shopping: who engages in it, and why. We examine the …rst by relating households' multistop shopping tendencies to their demographic and economic characteristics, and the second by comparing actual expenditures to those under a counterfactual one-stop scenario. The regression results indicate that multistop shopping is more prevalent among households with lower opportunity costs of time (due to unemployment or old age). Greater heterogeneity in stores'product o¤erings and higher in ‡ation-when adjusted for changes in shopping lists-are also associated with higher multistep shopping tendencies. The counterfactual analysis further shows that, for most trips, one-stop shopping would entail higher expenditures than the observed multistop trips. However, the magnitude of these savings is modest: households save between 4.7% and 11.5% of daily expenditures through multistop shopping.

title: The Influence Of E-Wallet on Consumer Spending Behavior at Tertiary Institution in Rural Areas of the Philippines
affiliations: Bukidnon State University, Bukidnon State University and Bukidnon State University

detail.title: The Influence Of E-Wallet on Consumer Spending Behavior at Tertiary Institution in Rural Areas of the Philippines
detail.abstract: The increasing use of e-wallets has reshaped financial transactions and purchasing behavior, particularly among students who value convenience, and accessibility. Despite their growing popularity, limited attention has been given to how e-wallet influences consumer spending behavior through peer and social factors. The paper aims to determine the extent of influence in perceived benefits, frequency of use, and transaction types on consumer spending behavior of college students at Bukidnon State University, Talisayan Campus. A descriptive-correlational design with multiple regression analysis was utilized, and data were collected from 89 BSBA students through a structured questionnaire. Descriptive findings shows that students highly valued convenience and accessibility, while buying load and transferring money emerged as the most common transaction. Regression analysis showed that perceived benefits and transaction types significantly influence consumer behavior, while frequency of use had no significant influence on the social aspect. The findings imply that e-wallets encourage peer and socially influenced spending behavior among students. It is recommended that financial literacy initiatives be strengthened to promote awareness and responsible digital spending habits.

title: The Politicisation of the UK's Prevent Counterterrorism Programme and why Adopting a New Public Health Model is Needed

detail.title: The Politicisation of the UK's Prevent Counterterrorism Programme and why Adopting a New Public Health Model is Needed

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: In the UK, Prevent is the countering and preventing violent extremism (P/CVE) strand of the national CONTEST counter-terrorism strategy. However, Prevent has disproportionately focused on Muslim communities, even amidst increasing evidence of the growing threats posed by other forms of radicalisation and violent extremism, particularly Extreme Far-Right ideologies and views. Prevent's narrow focus and politicisation have challenged its effectiveness and legitimacy with many key stakeholders. As a result, Prevent must be reoriented to adopt an innovative and original new public health model set out for the first time in this paper. Given the effectiveness of public health interventions for other forms of crime and violence epidemics, the proposed new public health model for Prevent is significant, as it could potentially increase programme effectiveness by addressing radicalisation and violent extremism risks across a wider variety of ideologies and beliefs, increasing legitimacy amongst essential practitioners and community stakeholders, and reducing politicisation.

title: Governing Customer-Facing AI: Valuing and Unlearning Data in Fine-Tuned Language Models
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business and University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Governing Customer-Facing AI: Valuing and Unlearning Data in Fine-Tuned Language Models

declarations.funderStatement: Y. Leng is supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) under [Grant IIS 2153468]

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to handle customer service and marketing communication. To perform well, these models are fine-tuned on proprietary interaction data. This creates a data-governance problem: training corpora are uneven in quality, and legal and contractual obligations give contributors growing control over how their data are used. Managers therefore need two operational capabilities: to quantify the record-level value of training data and to erase the influence of designated records from deployed models without costly retraining. We propose Low-Rank Directional Influence Tracing (LR-DIT), a data-governance framework for fine-tuned LLMs. LR-DIT represents training records and model outputs in a shared, low-dimensional semantic space, yielding interpretable record-level influence scores and a parameter update that selectively unlearns flagged records. In a large review platform that fine-tunes a reply model for merchant responses to consumer reviews, influence-guided corpus edits based on a small expert-labeled seed produce sizable gains in customer satisfaction and loyalty intentions, while a one-shot unlearning update approximates remove-and-retrain forgetting on targeted data with minimal drift elsewhere. LR-DIT thus helps treat training data as a measurable marketing asset and can make model editing and erasure more practical in customer-facing systems.

title: Analyzing the Significance of Islamic Marketing in Enhancing Halal Cosmetics Purchase Intention of Indonesian Muslim Gen Z
